巴拉萊卡琴以三根弦撥動發聲，其中兩根通常調成同音，第三根高純四度；三角空心木身提: The balalaika sounds from three strings, of which two are usually tuned alike and the third a perfect fourth above; the triangular hollow wooden body gives resonance, but the sound dies away quickly, so a melody often needs fast strumming or plucking to keep going. The high-pitched type has a higher range and mostly carries melody and chords; the middle and low types are larger, with longer and thicker strings and a lower range. The prima, secunda and alto can be played with the fingers or a pick, while the bass and contrabass use leather picks and stand on a foot, so that their volume and their long bass notes depend more on the material of the pick and the way it is used.
巴拉萊卡琴初學可先依三弦定音：兩條弦同音，第三弦高純四度。小型琴以手指或撥片彈奏: A beginner can start from the three-string tuning: two strings alike and the third a perfect fourth above. The small instruments are played with the fingers or a pick, and traditionally the side of the right index finger can sound the strings; the bass and contrabass stand on a foot on the floor and use a leather pick. Because the sustain is short, a melody needs fast strumming or plucking. The left hand stops the strings, and on the prima especially the thumb often presses the bass string to help shape a chord.
巴拉萊卡琴常見於俄國民樂與舞蹈伴奏，高音型負責旋律與和弦，因延音短需快速撥奏。巴: The balalaika is common in Russian folk music and dance accompaniment, where the high type carries melody and chords and, because the sustain is short, needs fast plucking. Balalaika orchestras play together in different sizes, performing classical music arranged for balalaika; Vasily Andreyev arranged traditional Russian folk songs and wrote concert pieces for it. In the Soviet period it also appeared in folk ensembles with the domra, gusli, bayan, Vladimir horn, garmoshka and percussion, and in the Red Army Choir's line-up of balalaikas and domras. Solo occasions include Alexei Arkhipovsky opening the second semi-final of the Eurovision Song Contest in Moscow.
巴拉萊卡琴是俄羅斯弦鳴樂器，霍恩博斯泰爾–薩克斯編號321.321，屬魯特琴類撥: The balalaika is a Russian chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 321.321, a plucked lute-type instrument and a member of the balalaika family. It has a triangular hollow wooden body, a fretted neck and three strings, usually two tuned alike with the third a perfect fourth above. The high type mostly plays melody and chords and, because the sustain is short, is often plucked or strummed quickly. Russian folk players use it for folk music and dance, and balalaika orchestras use it to play arranged classical music.
巴拉萊卡琴最早見於1688年逮捕文件，1700與1714年文件亦提及；1771年: The balalaika appears first in an arrest document of 1688, and is also mentioned in documents of 1700 and 1714; its name occurs in the 1771 poem Elysei. Early instruments had two to six strings, and in the nineteenth century it developed the triangular body and the shorter neck. In the 1880s Vasily Andreyev and the instrument maker Ivanov standardised the design, and Pasersky added fully chromatic frets and orchestral sizes. The Soviet period supported balalaika orchestras, and the Red Army Choir also switched to balalaikas and domras; interest in Russian folk instruments grew outside Russia in the twentieth century, helped by early Western tours by Andreyev and others.
巴拉萊卡琴為三角形中空木製琴身，面板多用雲杉、常綠樹或冷杉，背板由三至九片木段拼: The balalaika has a triangular hollow wooden body; the soundboard is mostly spruce, evergreen or fir, and the back is built from three to nine staves, usually maple. Early strings were gut, the thinnest melody string of stainless steel, and nylon is common today. Early frets were bound onto the neck with animal gut. The bass and contrabass are played with a leather pick, even leather from a shoe heel; the foot that supports them is a wooden or metal peg.
